oneSentence: Variance describes how much a fitted model’s predictions change when the same learning procedure is trained on slightly different samples.
plainExplanation:
Variance tells you how sensitive a fitted model is to changes in its training sample. If you train the same learning procedure on slightly different samples, a high-variance model may give noticeably different predictions each time. A low-variance model stays more stable.

To assess variance, repeat the same learning procedure with different training samples and compare the fitted models on the same cases or equivalent data. Fold-to-fold score changes are indirect evidence because validation folds can also differ. If the model fits accidental details specific to each training sample, its predictions may change substantially across fits.

Variance is often discussed with overfitting, but they are not identical. Overfitting means fitting training examples so closely that performance drops on new cases. High variance is one common reason for this because the fitted model is sensitive to the sample used.

Variance also differs from statistical bias and reliability. Statistical bias is systematic error caused by assumptions or structure that are too simple for the pattern. Reliability is broader consistency under comparable use. Variance specifically concerns changes caused by the training sample.

everydayAnalogy.title: Different clerks, slightly different piles
everydayAnalogy.story: A university receives 1,000 applications and asks several clerks to sort small samples into “complete” and “incomplete”. They all use the same checklist, but each clerk gets a slightly different pile of applications. If the checklist is clear and robust, the results look similar across piles. If the checklist relies on tiny quirks, one pile may look 92% complete and another only 74%, even though the overall applicant pool is similar.

everydayAnalogy.limitation: A real model does not literally follow a human checklist unless it was designed that way, and variance can appear even when the training procedure is fully automated. Also, in machine learning the instability often comes from mathematical fitting to limited data, not from people applying rules inconsistently.

visual.title: Low variance and high variance across repeated data splits
visual.learningObjective: Be able to explain that variance is about how much model results change across repeated, slightly different samples, and why that matters for trust in an evaluation score.
visual.description: Two side-by-side columns compare repeated evaluations of the same task. The left column shows similar scores across folds and stable decision boundaries; the right shows large score swings and shifting boundaries. Read top to bottom in each column, then compare the summary at the bottom.

steps.label: Same task, new samples
steps.explanation: Start with one prediction task and one modelling approach, but create several slightly different train/test splits from the same dataset.
steps.visualInstruction: At the top, draw one dataset box feeding into three smaller split boxes in each column. Use identical labels across columns: Split 1, Split 2, Split 3.

steps.label: Fit the model repeatedly
steps.explanation: Train the same kind of model on each split. Only the sampled data changes.
steps.visualInstruction: Under each split box, place a model icon with the same label. In the low-variance column, keep the model boundary lines visually similar; in the high-variance column, make them visibly different.

steps.label: Compare the scores
steps.explanation: Low variance gives similar validation scores across splits. High variance gives wide score swings, even though the task is unchanged.
steps.visualInstruction: Show score chips under each model. Left column example: 0.84, 0.83, 0.85. Right column example: 0.93, 0.71, 0.80. Use spacing and alignment, not colour alone, to show consistency versus spread.

steps.label: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: A single strong score is less convincing if repeated tests move a lot. Stable performance is usually easier to trust.
steps.visualInstruction: Add a bottom summary band in each column. Left: ‘stable estimate’. Right: ‘unstable estimate; possible overfitting’. Connect the score chips to the summary with thin lines.

visual.interaction: Hover or tap each split to highlight its decision boundary and score, then toggle an overlay that shows the score range across splits.
visual.accessibilityDescription: The diagram compares two ways the same model can behave across repeated train and test splits. In the left column, three slightly different data splits produce similar fitted boundaries and nearly identical scores, showing low variance. In the right column, the same process produces noticeably different boundaries and scores that vary widely, showing high variance. The message is that variance is about stability across samples: if results swing a lot, one good score may not represent real performance on new data.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static two-column comparison replaces animation. Each column shows three fixed split-model-score stacks and a final summary label. Consistency of the left scores and spread of the right scores are shown with printed values and a simple score-range bracket.

workedExample.scenario: A programme officer at Headquarters is testing a classifier that flags side-event concept notes missing required sections before they are circulated for clearance.
workedExample.input: A labelled archive of earlier concept notes, represented through text and layout features, is evaluated using repeated cross-validation.
process: The officer fits the same learning procedure several times, using slightly different training and validation samples.
The average F1 score appears acceptable, but the scores and individual flags differ markedly between folds.
An error review shows that the model relies heavily on rare template headings and formatting conventions that occur in only some samples.
The unstable features are removed, the model is simplified and the evaluation is repeated to check whether both predictions and fold-level results become more consistent.
workedExample.result: The large fold-to-fold spread is treated as evidence of high variance, rather than hidden behind the average. The revised model is considered stronger only if its performance remains reasonably stable when the training sample changes.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: At a lightly staffed field presence where the connection drops regularly, the ICT officer must send the front office, by close of business, talking points for informals on a proposed service that predicts network outages from monitoring logs.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: The officer checks whether fitting the same model on slightly different weeks of logs produces substantially different outage predictions. A respectable average score will not rescue the proposal if validation results swing widely depending on which weeks were used for training.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Network logs may reveal addresses, system topology and vulnerabilities. They must not be pasted into an external tool that is not approved for security-sensitive data, and credentials must never be included. Testing should use the approved environment, minimise exposed identifiers and restrict access to the file.

whyItMatters: A model can look strong because it scored well on one test, yet still be unreliable in practice if that score changes a lot with small data changes. Variance helps you ask a better question: not only “How high is the score?” but also “How stable is it?” This matters when choosing whether to deploy a system, compare vendors, set monitoring thresholds or trust a benchmark result. For non-specialists, variance is a warning sign against over-reading a single number. Stable performance is usually easier to defend, monitor and improve than performance that depends on a lucky split.
whereYouMayHearIt: During an ICT governance board review of cross-validation results
At a vendor demo, when the procurement unit asks why performance changes between test runs
In a regional bureau validation meeting before a model pilot is cleared
While a data focal point briefs the front office on unstable evaluation metrics

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Variance just means the model makes many mistakes.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Not exactly. A model can have a reasonable average error rate and still have high variance if that error rate changes a lot across different samples or runs. Variance is about instability, not simply the number of errors.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If one test score is very high, variance is not important.
commonMisconceptions.correction: A single high score may come from a favourable split, accidental patterns in the sample or data leakage. Without checking how results change across repeated evaluations, you cannot tell whether the score is representative.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Variance and statistical bias are the same thing.
commonMisconceptions.correction: They describe different problems. Statistical bias refers to systematic error from assumptions that are too rigid or miss the true pattern. Variance refers to sensitivity to the particular sample used. A model can be low in one and high in the other.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: More complex models always have lower variance because they fit the data better.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Complex models often fit the training data more closely, but that can make them more sensitive to sample-specific noise. Better fit on training data can therefore increase variance on new data rather than reduce it.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: Variance means the model’s results do not stay steady when you test it on slightly different data.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: In machine learning, variance is the component of error linked to sensitivity to fluctuations in the training sample. Formally, if you imagine repeatedly drawing datasets from the same underlying process and refitting the same learning algorithm, high variance means the learned function changes substantially across those draws. In practice, you often observe it indirectly through unstable validation metrics, shifting decision boundaries or large fold-to-fold differences under cross-validation. High variance is commonly associated with overfitting, because the model captures idiosyncratic features of the sample rather than reproducible signal. However, variance is not identical to overfitting, and it should be interpreted alongside bias, noise, leakage risk, class balance and the evaluation design.

keyTakeaway: A strong average score is not enough. If refitting the same procedure on slightly different samples changes predictions substantially, the model has high variance and may not generalise reliably.

quickCheck.question: Which result most strongly suggests high variance?
options: The model gets 82% accuracy on training data and 81% on test data from one fixed split.
Across five cross-validation folds, the F1 scores range from 0.93 down to 0.71 for the same model setup.
The model has lower recall than precision on a balanced test set.
The confusion matrix shows more false negatives than false positives in one evaluation run.
quickCheck.explanation: High variance appears as instability across repeated samples or splits. A wide spread in fold scores suggests the model’s apparent quality depends heavily on which data it saw. The other options may matter for other reasons, but they do not by themselves show instability across samples.

searchKeywords: what does variance mean in model evaluation

issues.problem: The page repeatedly defines variance as changes caused by training data, test samples or test splits. Model variance specifically concerns changes in the fitted predictor when the learning procedure is trained on different samples. Scores can change merely because test samples differ in difficulty or composition, even if the fitted model is unchanged. That is evaluation sampling variation, not necessarily model variance.
issues.fix: Use the corrected definitions below. State that fold-score instability is indirect evidence and compare predictions from repeated fits where possible.

issues.problem: The analogy does not represent model variance. Several clerks apply one fixed checklist to different piles, so changes in completeness rates can come from pile composition or clerk consistency. No new checklist is learned from each sample. The mapping nevertheless calls the checklist both the model structure and learned rules, which is false in the story and also blurs variance with reliability.
issues.fix: Change the title to “Different samples, different checklists”. Replace the story with: “A university uses several small samples from 1,000 applications to build checklists for classifying records as complete or incomplete. Each sample produces a new checklist. If the method learns broad patterns, the checklists classify a shared set similarly. If it learns sample-specific quirks, their classifications differ widely.” Map the samples to training samples, the resulting checklists to fitted models, and differences on the shared set to model variance.

issues.problem: The visual treats similar or widely spread validation scores as direct demonstrations of low or high model variance. Fold scores also depend on which cases are in each validation fold. The shifting fitted boundaries teach the mechanism, but the score language overstates what the scores alone establish.
issues.fix: Replace “Low variance gives similar validation scores across splits. High variance gives wide score swings” with “Similar scores are consistent with low variance. Wide swings can warn of high variance, but validation folds may also differ.” Change the right summary to “variable results; investigate variance”. In the accessibility description, say that shifting fitted boundaries show variance while score swings are supporting, indirect evidence.

issues.problem: The result moves too quickly from a large fold-score spread to high model variance. The arithmetic is correct: 0.91 + 0.74 + 0.88 + 0.76 + 0.90 = 4.19, and 4.19 / 5 = 0.838, which rounds to 0.84. However, fold differences alone do not isolate sensitivity of the fitted model from differences among validation folds.

The page claims distinction from reliability but then uses instability and “unreliable in practice” almost as synonyms for variance. Reliability is the broader consistency of result quality under comparable use. Variance is specifically sensitivity of fitted predictions to the training sample. The relationship needs to be stated rather than blurred.
